title: The Glymphatic System: From Basic Research Advances to Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation Applications-A Narrative Review.
first_affiliation: Department of Anesthesiology, Affiliated Hospital of Zunyi Medical University, 563100 Zunyi, Guizhou, China.

abstract.text: The glymphatic system (GS) is a pathway for waste clearance in the brain and a promising therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). GS function is governed by multiple interacting factors, such as aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarization, cerebral arterial pulsatility, and the integrity of meningeal lymphatic vessels (MLVs). Despite growing recognition of the importance of the GS, effective strategies to actively and non-invasively enhance glymphatic function have long been lacking. In recent years, non-invasive neuromodulatory approaches-most notably focused ultrasound (FUS), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM)-have emerged as novel strategies to modulate GS activity. Growing evidence suggests that these interventions can enhance glymphatic transport by influencing key regulatory mechanisms, including cerebrovascular dynamics, AQP4 expression and localization, and meningeal lymphatic drainage. In this review, we summarize current experimental advances in non-invasive, external alterations of the GS, discuss underlying mechanisms and translational challenges, and highlight the therapeutic potential of GS modulation in neurological diseases characterized by impaired waste clearance. However, further research about the function and dysfunction of the GS in humans is needed to evaluate the findings from animal studies and thereby fill the translational gap in the human pathophysiology of the GS.

title: Photobiomodulation Reduces Physiological Stress and Pain During Dental Diagnostic Procedures: The UM-DANE 1 Pediatric Clinical Trial.
first_affiliation: Clinical professor and chair, Department of Orthodontics and Pediatric Dentistry, University of Maryland School of Dentistry, Baltimore, MD, USA.

abstract.text: Purpose: To evaluate effectiveness of photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) in reducing physiological stress (as measured by heart rate [HR] change), self-reported pain, and anxiety during cold pulp testing and routine gingival probing in healthy school-aged children. Methods: This prospective, randomized, split-mouth clinical trial enrolled 30 children aged 7 to 12 years at the University of Maryland pediatric dental clinics from July 2025 to January 2026. Each participant received PBMT (multiwavelength LED device, Nuralyte™) on 1 primary molar and no treatment on the contralateral control tooth. Following a 2-minute waiting period, cold testing and gingival probing were performed. Primary outcomes were HR changes from baseline measured via pulse oximetry. Secondary outcomes included self-reported pain (Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale), anxiety (0 to 10 numeric rating scale), cold perception, cooperation level (Frankl scale), and duration of analgesia. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used for split-mouth comparisons. Results: PBMT significantly reduced HR changes during cold testing compared to control (2.23±8.95 versus 6.07±8.70 beats per minute [bpm]; mean difference=-3.83 bpm, 95% confidence interval=-6.89 to -0.77, P=0.016). For gingival probing, self-reported pain was significantly lower with PBMT (median within-subject difference -2.0 points, P=0.004). Sensory perception was preserved in both groups (93.3% positive cold response). Analgesic effects remained stable through 20 minutes post-application. No adverse events occurred. Conclusion: PBMT with a multi-wavelength near-infrared device reduced physiological stress and self-reported pain during pediatric dental diagnostic procedures while preserving sensory function, supporting its use as a promising nonpharmacological behavior guidance option.

title: Red Light Therapy and Mitochondrial Rejuvenation in Age-Related Disorders.
first_affiliation: The Student Scientific Society, Poznan University of Medical Sciences, 60-806, Poznan, Poland.

abstract.text: Aging is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired ATP production, and a decline in tissue regenerative capacity, leading to the development of age-related diseases. This review summarizes current evidence regarding the effects of photobiomodulation (PBM) on mitochondrial function and age-related disorders. PBM using red and near-infrared light may enhance proper mitochondrial function by acting on cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) and other signaling pathways, including the transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel, leading to increased ATP production, modulation of ROS signaling, and improved cellular homeostasis. We review in vitro, animal, and clinical studies investigating PBM in metabolic, neurodegenerative, hepatic, cardiovascular, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and skeletal muscle disorders associated with aging, as well as its application in the management of cancer therapy-related oral mucositis. Current studies demonstrate beneficial effects on glucose metabolism, cardiovascular function, neuronal function, lipid metabolism, liver function, muscle regeneration, and visual function in AMD, as well as the safety and efficacy of PBM in the management of cancer therapy-induced oral mucositis. The therapeutic effects of PBM appear to be dose-dependent and influenced by treatment parameters including wavelength, fluence, irradiance, and exposure protocol. Although photobiomodulation still lacks standardized treatment protocols and differences exist in the wavelengths used, dosage, and frequency among studies, it represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of age-related diseases.

title: Transcranial photobiomodulation mitigates anxiety and depression-like behavior by modulation of mitochondrial and neuroinflammatory pathways in a mouse model of simulated microgravity.
journal: Journal of photochemistry and photobiology. B, Biology
first_affiliation: Neurosciences Research Center, Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran.

abstract.text: Mental health is a major concern for astronauts due to the high risk of anxiety and depression caused by prolonged exposure to microgravity and the stresses of spaceflight. Existing pharmacological treatments are inadequate for space missions, emphasizing the necessity for safe, noninvasive interventions. This study explored the therapeutic efficacy of transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM) using near-infrared (NIR) light therapy on mood regulation and the neurobiological mechanisms in mice subjected to simulated microgravity. Male mice were divided into three groups: a control group, a hindlimb unloading (HU) group subjected to 28 days of unloading, and an HU + tPBM group receiving daily tPBM treatment at 810 nm. The forced swim and tail suspension tests were employed to evaluate depressive-like behavior, while the elevated plus maze and open field tests were employed to measure anxiety-like behavior. Biochemical analysis of prefrontal cortex samples assessed mitochondrial bioenergetics (cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5 A [Cox5A], NADH dehydrogenase activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP), oxidative stress markers (NADPH oxidase 2 [NOX2], reactive oxygen species [ROS], and antioxidant activity), as well as neuroinflammatory mediators (toll-like receptor 4 [TLR4], phosphorylated mitogen-activated protein kinase [p-MAPK], phosphorylated nuclear factor kappa-B [p-NF-κB], interleukin-1β, and interferon-γ). HU provoked behavior resembling anxiety and depression, along with increased corticosterone levels, compromised mitochondrial function, increased NOX2 and ROS levels, and activated TLR4/MAPK/NF-κB signaling. Notably, tPBM reversed these changes, restored mitochondrial bioenergetics, diminished oxidative stress, and suppressed neuroinflammation, leading to considerable behavioral improvement. These findings indicate that tPBM may represent a promising, non-invasive approach for ameliorating mental health issues during long-duration spaceflight.

title: Photobiomodulation in Parkinson's disease: From pathogenesis to intervention.
first_affiliation: Laboratory of Exercise and Neurobiology, School of Physical Education and Sports Science, South China Normal University, Guangzhou, 510006, China.

abstract.text: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder clinically characterized by bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and postural instability. Its core pathological features include the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons within the substantia nigra pars compacta, striatal dopamine depletion, and intracellular accumulation of misfolded α-Synuclein (α-Syn)-rich Lewy inclusions that trigger neuronal dysfunction and cell death. Despite substantial research efforts, existing pharmacological strategies targeting α-Syn and dopaminergic neurons show limited capacity to halt or reverse PD progression, creating an urgent need for novel alternative therapeutic interventions. Photobiomodulation (PBM) is a non-invasive phototherapy that delivers photonic energy to biological tissues using visible and near-infrared light. Preclinical studies have documented neuroprotective signals linked to PBM in experimental PD models; however, clinical studies to date provide only preliminary and inconsistent evidence regarding safety and possible symptomatic benefit. This narrative review outlines the mechanistic rationale, preclinical findings, clinical observations, and key translational limitations for PBM as an investigational adjunctive intervention in PD. We first elaborate on PD-related pathological mechanisms, followed by an in-depth discussion of PBM-mediated biological actions, and consolidate recent evidence for its anti-PD applications in preclinical settings. Available preclinical data suggest PBM could modulate mitochondrial function, neuroinflammation, dopaminergic-neuron survival, and responses along the microbiota-gut-brain axis in experimental PD models, though direct evidence supporting modification of α-synuclein aggregation or propagation remains sparse. Clinical observations support procedural feasibility and acceptable short-term safety profiles. Nevertheless, definitive clinical efficacy cannot be confirmed given small sample sizes, heterogeneous intervention protocols, and inconsistent outcomes from controlled trials. PBM should currently be regarded as an investigational adjunctive strategy rather than an established therapy for PD.

title: Cerebral blood flow in remitted bipolar disorder after transcranial infrared laser stimulation measured by arterial spin labeling MRI.
first_affiliation: Bipolar Disorder Center, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Dell Medical School, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, 78712, United States.

abstract.text: Bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with cognitive impairment even during remitted states. Evidence suggests that these deficits may be linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and reduced metabolic activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), which may manifest as altered cerebral blood flow (CBF). Transcranial infrared laser stimulation (TILS) is a non-invasive photobiomodulation technique that targets the and may enhance mitochondrial activity through stimulation of cytochrome c oxidase, thereby increasing metabolic energy production and tissue oxygenation. However, the effects of TILS on brain perfusion in BD have not been well characterized. This study examined the effects of repeated TILS administration on CBF using arterial spin-labeled (ASL) MRI in individuals with remitted BD. Twenty-nine participants with BD received six weekly TILS sessions targeting bilateral frontopolar regions (Brodmann area 10). MRI scans were conducted at baseline, within 24 hours following the first TILS session, and within 24 hours after the sixth session. Repeated-measures ANOVA assessed CBF changes across time while controlling for bipolar subtype, age, and sex. Results revealed a significant acute increase in CBF following the first TILS session in the left superior frontal gyrus (BA10) and left orbital frontal cortex (BA11), followed by a significant decrease after six weeks of treatment. A decrease in CBF from session one to session six was also observed in the right anterior cingulate gyrus (BA32). These findings suggest a biphasic response to TILS and support further investigation of TILS as a potential intervention for cognitive impairment in BD.

title: Non-invasive neuromodulation after repetitive head impacts: current evidence and a precision framework for circuit-based rehabilitation.
first_affiliation: School of Psychology, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Repetitive head impacts (RHIs) are associated with heterogeneous cognitive, behavioral, psychiatric, sleep-related, pain, and neurological symptoms. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) remains a postmortem neuropathological diagnosis, whereas traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES) is a clinical research syndrome assessed during life. No intervention has been shown to modify CTE pathology, but neuromodulation may support the surviving neural circuits.

abstract.label: AREAS COVERED
abstract.text: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar were searched from database inception to August 2026 for this narrative review. The author evaluates magnetic and electrical stimulation, low-intensity ultrasound, photobiomodulation and cranial nerve stimulation as adjuncts to rehabilitation after repetitive head impacts. Direct RHI/TES evidence is distinguished from findings in other traumatic brain injury and concussion populations, other clinical populations and experimental models. The author then proposes a phenotype- and circuit-guided framework for treatment development.

abstract.label: EXPERT OPINION
abstract.text: Neuromodulation should not be considered a disease-modifying treatment for CTE. Its most credible role is as a phenotype-led adjunct to rehabilitation. This approach requires identification of a viable circuit relevant to the dominant impairment, selection of an individualized stimulation dose, measurement of target engagement and pairing with symptom-relevant rehabilitation. Progress requires credible sham-controlled and factorial trials, multimodal biomarkers, clinically meaningful functional outcomes, and long-term follow-up.

title: Effects of melatonin and transcranial photobiomodulation on neuroinflammation-related gene expression and anxiety-like behaviors in rats under chronic restraint stress.
first_affiliation: Applied Physiology Research Center, Cardiovascular Research Institute, Isfahan University of Medical Sciences, Isfahan, Iran.

abstract.text: Psychological stress causes immunological and behavioral alterations that can maladaptively affect the quality of life. However, melatonin (MLT) and transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM) have promising effects on brain functions. This study investigated the effects of MLT and tPBM in rats under chronic stress by evaluating neuroinflammation-related gene expression and anxiety-like behaviors. Sixty-three male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to nine groups: Control (Co), Sham injection (Sh-I), Sham tPBM (Sh-tPBM), MLT, tPBM, Stress (St), Stress with Melatonin (St-MLT), Stress with tPBM (St-tPBM), and Stress with Melatonin and tPBM (St-MLT-tPBM). Chronic restraint stress (2 h/day for 21 days) was applied to all stressed rats. MLT (20 mg/kg; intraperitoneal) and tPBM (808 nm; delivered to the scalp surface) were administered following restraint stress. Gene expression of hippocampal neuroinflammation-associated genes (IL-17A, ICAM-1, VCAM-1, IL-1β, and Aif1) was measured by real-time PCR. Additionally, anxiety-like behaviors were evaluated by the elevated-plus maze test. Hippocampal IL-17A and ICAM-1 gene expression was higher in stressed rats than in normal subjects. However, in the St group, IL-1β expression remained unchanged, whereas Aif1 expression was decreased compared with the Co group. tPBM reversed the stress-induced upregulation of IL-17A and ICAM-1 expression, whereas MLT could not mitigate them compared with normal subjects. The combined MLT and tPBM treatment elicited gene expression changes similar to those observed with tPBM alone. Stress-induced anxiety-like behaviors were significantly reduced by MLT, with effects similar to those of the combined treatment, which outperformed tPBM alone. These findings suggest the potential of tPBM and melatonin as complementary approaches for mitigating stress-related alterations, highlighting further investigation to optimize their doses and treatment parameters.

title: Transcranial Photobiomodulation Attenuates Neurogenic Inflammation and Sensory Hypersensitivity in a Nitroglycerin-Induced Migraine Model: Toward a Nonpharmacological Therapy.
first_affiliation: Neurosciences Research Center, Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran, tbzmed.ac.ir.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Migraine is a debilitating neurological condition, characterized by headache, photophobia, and heightened mechanical/thermal sensitivity. Current pharmacological therapies often lead to incomplete relief and adverse effects, necessitating the use of noninvasive alternatives. This study evaluated transcranial photobiomodulation (PBM) in a nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced migraine model in male mice.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Mice were assigned to Sham, NTG, NTG + Sumatriptan (SUMA; 600 µg/kg, s.c.), NTG + PBM, and NTG + PBM + SUMA groups. Over 9 days, NTG (5 mg/kg) was injected intraperitoneally every other day to develop an animal model of chronic migraine. The PBM protocol involved daily irradiation (810 nm) on the occipital bone of the head for 5 s over 9 days. The animals underwent behavioral testing for photophobia, mechanical allodynia, and thermal sensitivity. The trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) was assessed for miR-155 expression by real-time PCR and protein expression of phospho-NF-κB, IL-1β, transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) and vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), c-Fos, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) using immunoblotting.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Behavioral assessment revealed that PBM significantly reduced head scratching and improved exploratory activity, decreased light aversion, reversed periorbital/hindpaw mechanical allodynia, and prolonged thermal withdrawal latency compared to the NTG group. Moreover, PBM downregulated miR-155 expression and decreased levels of inflammatory mediators and migraine-associated neuropeptides in the TNC. Notably, combined PBM and SUMA treatment resulted in improvements in behavioral and molecular outcomes compared to either treatment alone.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These results indicate that PBM inhibited migraine-like behaviors and decreased the expression of numerous molecular markers that are linked to neuroinflammation and trigeminal activation in the TNC. These findings establish a foundation for additional research on transcranial PBM as a noninvasive method for modulating migraine-related behavioral responses.

title: A Review of the Molecular Evidence for Near-Infrared Light in Astrocyte-Mediated Neurorehabilitation.
first_affiliation: Key Laboratory of Experimental Teratology of the Ministry of Education, Department of Medical Genetics, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Cheeloo College of Medicine, Shandong University, Jinan, 250012, Shandong, China. lixi@sdu.edu.cn.

abstract.text: Near-infrared (NIR) light represents a promising, noninvasive therapeutic for neurological disorders, predicated on its capacity to modulate astrocyte function. As the primary glial population in the central nervous system, astrocytes are indispensable for maintaining neuronal homeostasis, regulating glutamate metabolism, and supporting metabolic energetics. This review synthesizes recent advancements in NIR-driven neurorehabilitation, elucidating the molecular signaling cascades and transduction pathways activated within the astrocytic network. We specifically examine translational applications across preclinical and clinical models of stroke, Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy, and psychiatric disorders. Furthermore, we evaluate how the integration of optogenetic tools and nanomaterials has refined NIR therapies, establishing a foundation for high-precision neurology. Given the rising demand for nonsurgical interventions, this review provides a timely framework for the next generation of photobiomodulation and neural modulation strategies.

title: Targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's and Parkinson´s disease: recent therapeutic approaches.
first_affiliation: Department of Informatics and Microsystems and Technology, University of Applied Sciences Kaiserslautern, Zweibrücken, Germany.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) are the most common neurodegenerative disorders with limited disease-modifying treatment options. Evidence suggests that the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA) plays a role in these diseases by facilitating communication between the gut and the central nervous system. Associations have been found between altered gut microbiota composition and function, impaired barrier integrity, dysregulated metabolite production, and immune activation to neuroinflammation and progressive neurodegeneration.

abstract.label: AREAS COVERED
abstract.text: This review summarizes and critically assesses recent studies from the past year to provide an updated overview of therapeutic strategies targeting the MGBA in both diseases. We discuss dietary interventions, probiotics, postbiotics, microbial metabolites, and approaches targeting gut barrier function. We also highlight strategies such as fecal transplantation, photobiomodulation, and PD-targeted metabolism therapies using butyrate and resistant starch.

abstract.label: EXPERT OPINION
abstract.text: While these interventions have shown promising results in preclinical and early clinical trials, their clinical application is limited by methodological heterogeneity, interindividual variability, and a lack of standardized protocols. Successful implementation requires carefully designed clinical trials, particularly longitudinal studies of presymptomatic cohorts, standardized microbiome analyses, and integrated multi-omics approaches to elucidate causal relations and facilitate personalized treatment strategies.

title: Photobiomodulation as a regulator of neuroinflammation: mechanistic insights and therapeutic potential in brain disorders.
first_affiliation: REGEnLIFE, Paris, France.

abstract.text: Brain disorders, including neurodegenerative, neuropsychiatric, and cerebrovascular diseases, represent a growing global health challenge contributing to disability and mortality worldwide. Although these conditions differ in etiology and clinical presentation, accumulating evidence identifies neuroinflammation as a shared pathological mechanism. Involving microglial activation, astrocytic reactivity, cytokine dysregulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption, it contributes to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal loss, and disease progression, yet therapeutic strategies targeting these processes remain limited. Photobiomodulation (PBM), the therapeutic application of low-intensity red to near-infrared light, has emerged as a neurotechnology capable of modulating biological pathways relevant to neuroinflammation. Preclinical studies suggest that PBM may influence mitochondrial activity through cytochrome c oxidase-mediated mechanisms, enhancing cellular metabolism while regulating reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signaling pathways, and tissue homeostasis. Through these effects, PBM may attenuate neuroinflammatory responses, regulate glial activation, and support neuroprotective processes across multiple neurological models. This narrative review examines evidence supporting neuroinflammation as a common denominator across major brain disorders and explores the biological rationale for PBM as a therapeutic strategy. It summarizes the cellular and molecular basis of PBM, its effects on neuroinflammatory pathways, and preclinical and clinical findings across brain disease models. Preclinical findings consistently support a multi-target anti-inflammatory effect, whereas clinical investigation remains at an early stage, with encouraging results in Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis but mainly negative data on primary outcomes in Parkinson's disease and major depressive disorder. Further research is needed to optimize treatment parameters, clarify mechanisms of action, and determine clinical efficacy across disease contexts.

title: Transcranial photobiomodulation reduces predator-induced anxiety-like behavior (risk assessment) in male Rattus norvegicus threatened by Bothrops jararaca pit vipers.
first_affiliation: Laboratory of Neuroanatomy and Neuropsychobiology, Department of Pharmacology, Ribeirão Preto Medical School of the University of São Paulo (FMRP-USP), Ribeirão Preto, Brazil.

abstract.text: Photobiomodulation, also known as low-level laser therapy, uses specific wavelengths of light to stimulate biological tissues. Evidence from the literature indicates that transcranial photobiomodulation can alter neurophysiological activity; however, studies investigating its effects on the neurobiology of emotions remain scarce. Therefore, the objective of the present study was to investigate the effects of acute transcranial photobiomodulation administered at five irradiation sites using an 808 nm (± 10 nm) wavelength on anxiety-like behavior in rodents (Rattus norvegicus) exposed to either a potential wild predator (Bothrops jararaca) or predator-related cues (snake odor). Both the presence of the snake and exposure to its odor elicited anxiety-like risk-assessment behavior in the rodents. In turn, photobiomodulation treatment significantly reduced both the frequency and duration of this behavior, suggesting a potential anxiolytic-like effect.

title: Editorial: Photobiomodulation therapy for brain disorders, volume II.
first_affiliation: Laboratory of Exercise and Neurobiology, School of Physical Education and Sports Science, South China Normal University, Guangzhou, China.

title: The evolution of direct transcranial photobiomodulation: a history of dose, depth, and delivery.
first_affiliation: NeuroThera, Newark, DE, United States.

abstract.text: Direct transcranial photobiomodulation (dtPBM) delivers red or near-infrared light through the scalp and skull with the aim of affecting brain tissue. The field has produced encouraging findings but inconsistent clinical results. We reconstruct its development as a history of scientific and engineering decisions in which optical access, target depth, and dose repeatedly shaped what could be tested. The clinical lineage began with light therapy for ischemic myocardium and moved to stroke, where cadaver measurements established that near-infrared light could traverse the human scalp and skull and defined a historical design target of approximately 7.5 mW/cm2 at the dura. The NEST clinical program then carried a fixed 808-nm regimen into three stroke trials: NEST-1 met its primary endpoint, NEST-2 showed a nonsignificant overall trend (p = 0.094) with a published post hoc signal in moderate stroke (p = 0.044), and NEST-3 stopped for futility. An unpublished, exploratory NEST-2 reanalysis described larger treatment differences for superficial lesions; this observation motivates prospective testing but does not establish depth-dependent efficacy. After NEST, treatment moved to the forehead, where target geometry was more reproducible. The ELATED trials adopted a more practical LED platform at substantially lower irradiance while preserving broadly similar treatment-site radiant exposure, whereas the TRIADE R61 trial deliberately varied optical parameters and found optical-parameter-dependent, bidirectional BOLD power responses. The historical record also leaves biological mechanism unresolved: mitochondrial/redox, neurovascular, glial-inflammatory, network-mediated, and diffuse or systemic pathways remain plausible at different levels of evidence, and a distributed physiological response does not by itself identify where the effect begins. These observations support a constrained historical inference: dose, depth, and delivery site are biological variables, not merely device specifications. We distinguish focal-local, diffuse/systemic, and local-stimulation/network-mediated accounts of action and identify prospective tests that can discriminate among them. The next phase of dtPBM development should prioritize indications in which optical access, target engagement, and a disease-relevant network or biomarker can be specified prospectively rather than inferred after a clinical outcome.

title: Neuromodulatory interventions for Alzheimer's disease.
first_affiliation: School of Advanced Technology, Algonquin College, Ottawa, ON, Canada.

abstract.text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent an escalating global public health challenge with major socioeconomic consequences. Although anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies have introduced disease-modifying treatment options for early symptomatic AD, their benefits remain modest and must be balanced against cost, monitoring burden, and safety risks. Neuromodulatory interventions have therefore emerged as promising investigational strategies that may complement existing therapeutic approaches. This narrative review evaluates current clinical and neurophysiological evidence for seven major neuromodulation approaches: 40 Hz gamma rhythm sensory stimulation, also known as gamma entrainment using sensory stimulation (GENUS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), focused ultrasound (FUS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM). Integrating clinical findings with mechanistic evidence, we examine synaptic plasticity, neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance, oscillatory entrainment, and cholinergic signaling as candidate therapeutic mechanisms. A comparative matrix summarizes target specificity, invasiveness, stimulation parameters, and translational status. Finally, we discuss key barriers, including biological heterogeneity, protocol standardization, durability of benefit, caregiver burden, and the uncertain implications of continuous network stimulation for future personalized and closed-loop interventions.

title: From pathogenesis to non-medical therapy: A review of exploring sensory and multi-sensory stimulation as a non-invasive treatment approach for Alzheimer's disease.
first_affiliation: Douglas Research Centre, Department of Psychiatry, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada.

abstract.text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, marked by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction, ultimately leading to memory loss, cognitive decline, neuropsychiatric symptoms and neuronal degeneration that impairs daily functioning. Despite the availability of pharmacological treatments developed to slow down symptom progression, their clinical efficacy remains uncertain, and they are frequently associated with adverse side effects, underscoring the urgent demand for safer and more effective therapeutic alternatives. Non-pharmacological approaches, therefore, have been investigated and are considered promising alternative therapeutic strategies for AD. This paper outlines the pathological features and neural network changes that occur across the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD), reviews the effects of different sensory stimulation approaches on reducing these AD-associated changes, and discusses the potential mechanisms underlying various sensory and multisensory stimulation interventions in mitigating AD-related symptoms. These sensory stimulation interventions, including 40 Hz Gamma Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation [GENUS], Photobiomodulation, Bright Light Therapy, Music Therapy, Aromatherapy, Tactile Stimulation, and Multisensory Stimulation, are found to slow down the progression of AD by ameliorating multiple AD pathologies, enhancing cognitive function, promoting neuroplasticity, regulating sleep patterns, and reducing behavioural or neuropsychiatric symptoms. Crucially, this present work integrates both human and animal studies, aligning clinical outcomes with mechanistic insights derived from animal studies, thereby bridging preclinical and clinical research to promote the translation of sensory interventions into effective treatments for patients with AD.

title: Photobiomodulation Ameliorates Alexander Disease Through AMPK/mTOR-Mediated Mitophagy.
first_affiliation: Department of Neurobiology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, National Institute on Drug Dependence, Peking University, Beijing, China.

abstract.text: Alexander disease (AxD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the pathological accumulation of Rosenthal fibers (RFs) and astrocytic inflammation. Despite advances in elucidating its genetic basis, effective therapeutic strategies remain limited. Recent studies indicate that astrocytes in AxD exhibit excessive mitochondrial fragmentation, which may cause mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory response. Photobiomodulation (PBM) has been shown to improve mitochondrial function and exert anti-inflammatory effects, suggesting it may be a promising candidate for the treatment of AxD. Here, we report that exposure to 1070-nm infrared light exerts therapeutic efficacy in AxD. Specifically, using the astrocytes derived from AxD patients and a mouse model of AxD, we demonstrate that PBM regulates AMPK/mTOR signaling and promotes mitophagy, thereby attenuating reactive oxygen species production from fragmented mitochondria and subsequent inflammatory status. This study suggests PBM may serve as a novel, non-invasive therapeutic approach for the treatment of AxD.

title: Non-invasive neuromodulation in Alzheimer's disease: toward brain-heart coupling as a candidate framework for biomarker-guided adaptive intervention.
first_affiliation: School of Electrical Engineering, Hebei University of Technology, Tianjin, 300401, China.

abstract.text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) has entered an era of biologically informed, disease-modifying therapy, yet durable clinical benefit remains limited, highlighting the need for complementary interventions. Noninvasive neuromodulation has emerged as a promising strategy, but the field is still largely organized by device categories, stimulation targets, and short-term cognitive outcomes. This framing alone does not readily account for the marked heterogeneity, stage dependence, and limited durability reported across studies. This narrative review synthesizes clinical, preclinical, and mechanistic evidence across repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcranial electrical stimulation, sensory gamma entrainment, focused ultrasound, photobiomodulation, and transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation. We propose that device classification is a useful starting point but an incomplete explanatory framework, because different modalities have been linked, with varying levels of evidence, to overlapping processes involving network reconfiguration, autonomic regulation, neurovascular function, inflammatory signaling, and clearance-related biology. Against this background, we examine the brain-heart axis and the central autonomic network (CAN) as a candidate intermediate level at which central neural and peripheral physiological responses to stimulation might be jointly characterized. Building on this view, we propose a biomarker hierarchy that extends from heart rate variability to directional and time-varying brain-heart coupling measures, which could be tested as candidate markers of physiological state, target engagement, and treatment responsiveness. At present, however, there is no prospective evidence that brain-heart coupling causally mediates the therapeutic effects of neuromodulation in AD. We, therefore, present brain-heart coupling as a testable candidate framework for studying state dependence, target engagement, and, ultimately, biomarker-guided adaptive neuromodulation.

title: Photobiomodulation: multifaceted therapeutic effects on disorders in the central nervous system.
first_affiliation: Department of Geriatrics, Seventh Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, Shenzhen 518107, China.

abstract.text: Conventional pharmacological interventions for brain diseases are often limited by complex pathophysiological mechanisms, suboptimal efficacy, and pronounced side effects. In contrast, photobiomodulation (PBM) has attracted increasing attention due to its non-invasive nature, multi-target effects, and favourable safety profile. In brain diseases, PBM employs specific light wavelengths to activate mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase and photosensitive proteins and to regulate neuronal oscillatory activity and neuroglial functions. Human studies demonstrated the efficacy of PBM in improving cognitive performance, motor symptoms, and emotional distress in patients with neurodegenerative diseases, brain trauma, and psychiatric disorders. Therapeutic outcomes are influenced by key parameters of the protocol, such as wavelength, dosage, and frequency, as well as inter-individual variability in anatomical and physiological factors. Future research needs to focus on establishing a database of disease-specific parameters to enable personalised treatment protocols by integrating imaging and molecular biomarkers and performing large-scale clinical trials to validate long-term safety and translational potential.

title: The Role of Photobiomodulation Therapy in Enhancing Neurogenesis: Mechanisms and Applications.
first_affiliation: School of Physical Education and Sports Science, South China Normal University, Guangzhou, China.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Adult neurogenesis, critical for neural repair and functional plasticity, is impaired in neurological disorders including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and traumatic brain injury (TBI).

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This review summarizes the physiological basis of adult neurogenesis and photobiomodulation (PBM) fundamentals, clarifies PBM-induced neurogenesis mechanisms, evaluates its pre-clinical/clinical efficacy and safety, and addresses translational challenges to support clinical translation.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: We synthesized relevant literature, covering adult neurogenesis characteristics, PBM principles/mechanisms, pre-clinical studies in disorder models, clinical safety/efficacy data, and comparisons with conventional neurogenic therapies.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: PBM promotes neurogenesis via regulating neural stem cell activity, mitochondrial function, and oxidative stress. Pre-clinical/clinical evidence confirms its safety and efficacy; despite parameter and long-term safety challenges, it has great potential in neuroregenerative medicine.

title: Neuromodulation for post-stroke aphasia rehabilitation: established cortical stimulation and emerging network-based targets.
first_affiliation: Department of Humanities Studies, University of Naples Federico II, Naples, Italy.

abstract.text: Post-stroke aphasia is a disabling disorder of language and communication for which speech-language therapy remains the standard of care. Because behavioural treatment yields variable gains and many people retain chronic communication limitations, non-invasive neuromodulation has been investigated to increase the responsiveness of residual language networks to therapy. This narrative review critically integrates evidence available through July 2026 for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), theta-burst stimulation, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), and emerging approaches targeting the cerebellum, spinal sensorimotor pathways, and cellular metabolism. Recent meta-analyses support small-to-moderate average benefits of adjunctive cortical stimulation, especially for naming, but these estimates coexist with marked heterogeneity, small trials and incomplete evidence for generalisation, durability, functional communication, and quality of life. Recent randomised studies illustrate the value of pairing stimulation with a defined learning task and of using lesion, tract, functional-connectivity, or hemodynamic information to select targets and predict response. Cerebellar tDCS, transcutaneous spinal direct current stimulation, transcranial alternating current stimulation, and transcranial photobiomodulation are conceptually attractive but remain investigational because the clinical evidence is limited, inconsistent, or based on uncontrolled and proof-of-concept studies. Across modalities, serious adverse events are uncommon when contemporary screening and dosing guidance are followed, although stroke-specific comorbidity and seizure risk require trained supervision. Neuromodulation should therefore be viewed as a potentially useful, state-dependent amplifier of speech-language therapy rather than a replacement for it. Progress towards routine care will require adequately powered multisite trials, preregistered patient-level stratification, treatment-fidelity reporting, ecologically valid outcomes, longer follow-up, and direct comparisons of personalised with fixed protocols.

title: Bilateral Angular Gyrus 810-nm Transcranial Near-Infrared Stimulation Reshapes Brain Network: Ameliorate Alzheimer's Disease Cognitive Deficits.
first_affiliation: Department of Neurology, The First Hospital of Hebei Medical University, Shijiazhuang, China.

abstract.text: Objective: To investigate the clinical efficacy and neural mechanisms of targeted 810-nm transcranial near-infrared stimulation (tNIRS) over the bilateral angular gyrus in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Impact Statement: We provide the first clinical evidence that targeted tNIRS ameliorates AD cognitive deficits by dynamically reconfiguring large-scale brain networks, establishing a precise, mechanistic neuromodulation strategy. Introduction: While tNIRS shows potential for AD, conventional whole-brain irradiation lacks anatomical precision and yields inconsistent outcomes. Resolving these elusive network-level mechanisms requires targeted stimulation paradigms. Methods: In a randomized, sham-controlled trial, 36 biomarker-confirmed AD patients received 810-nm tNIRS targeted at the bilateral angular gyrus or sham stimulation (20 min/side daily, 15 d). Baseline and post-intervention neuropsychological assessments, resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation-electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) were utilized to decode cognitive improvements and network dynamics. Results: Targeted tNIRS obviously improved cognition, memory, language, attention, and executive functions while reducing neuropsychiatric symptoms. fMRI revealed enhanced intra-network connectivity within the default mode network (DMN) and promoted functional synergy between the DMN, dorsal attention, frontoparietal, and limbic networks. TMS-EEG demonstrated enhanced information flow and dynamic nodal reconfiguration, specifically boosting prefrontal and temporo-occipital activation. Conclusion: Bilateral angular gyrus targeted tNIRS may effectively mitigate AD cognitive impairment potentially through modulation of functional connectivity and adaptively reconfiguring higher-order cognitive networks, serving as a highly promising clinical neuromodulation therapy.

title: Brain photobiomodulation therapy for acute sport-related concussion: a randomized, single-blinded, pilot clinical trial (RECOVERY study).
first_affiliation: Georges Pompidou European Hospital, Paris, France.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The current standard of care for concussion relies on symptom management; there are almost no disease-modifying treatments. The RECOVERY study investigated the safety of RGn550 (REGEnLIFE), a novel neurostimulation device combining brain photobiomodulation with a static magnetic field, in sportspeople with acute concussion and described concussion-related parameters in patients receiving this therapy.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective, randomized (central randomization, 1:1 ratio), single-blind, monocentric, pilot study compared two pulse frequencies (5 Hz and 10 Hz). Adult sportspeople with a concussion from a shock during sport practice occurring less than 72 h before inclusion were treated for 20 min at day 0 (D0) and D7 and followed up to D52. The primary outcome was the incidence of adverse device effects (ADEs). The secondary outcomes evaluated oculomotor, balance and executive function, concussion symptoms, and blood markers. The sample size was determined by the probability of observing at least one ADE, while all secondary analyses were exploratory and unadjusted for multiplicity.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Fifty patients were included, randomized, and treated at least once with 5 Hz (n = 26) or 10 Hz (n = 24); 49 (98.0%) of them completed the study. No difference was detected between the groups for primary or secondary outcomes. At least one ADE occurred in 38.5% (n = 10) [CI95: 20.2; 59.4] in the 5 Hz group and 41.7% (n = 10) [CI95: 22.1; 63.4] in the 10 Hz group. All ADEs were mild, non-serious (e.g., somnolence and medical device site discomfort), and resolved. Changes in several secondary outcomes were observed over the follow-up period, including within-visit changes in oculomotor measures.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: No difference in tolerability was detected between the 5 and 10 Hz modalities, although the study was neither designed nor powered to establish equivalence. Both conditions were well tolerated. In the absence of a sham comparator, secondary outcome data are hypothesis-generating and cannot be described in terms of efficacy. However, these data still provide the feasibility and variability estimates required to design an adequately powered, double-blind, sham-controlled trial in an indication that currently lacks disease-modifying treatment.

abstract.label: CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05647304, NCT05647304.

title: Photobiomodulation Irradiation Protocols for Burning Mouth Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Protocol-Level Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
first_affiliation: Department of Oral Medicine, Dental and Life Science Institute, School of Dentistry, Pusan National University, Yangsan-si, Republic of Korea.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To evaluate the effects of photobiomodulation therapy/low-level laser therapy (PBMT/LLLT) on burning mouth syndrome (BMS) and to explore whether irradiation protocol variables modify treatment effects.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Randomized controlled trials were synthesized according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) and Cochrane guidance. The protocol was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (CRD420261329136). Random-effects meta-analyses evaluated pain, Oral Health Impact Profile-14 (OHIP-14), xerostomia, anxiety, and depression. Irradiation-related subgroup analyses, including wavelength, power, fluence, irradiation time, session frequency, treatment duration, and application mode, were exploratory.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eighteen trials were included. PBMT/LLLT reduced pain (mean difference [MD] -1.09, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.60 to -0.57; I2 = 89%) and improved OHIP-14 (MD -3.82, 95% CI: -4.79 to -2.86; I2 = 41%). Xerostomia and depression were not significantly improved, whereas anxiety showed a modest reduction. Several irradiation protocol variables showed nominal exploratory signals.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: PBMT/LLLT may reduce BMS-related pain and improve oral-health-related quality of life. Current evidence supports irradiation protocol standardization but remains insufficient to define an optimal protocol.

title: Use of neurostimulation in patients with treatment-resistant depression: current options and future directions.
first_affiliation: Department of Psychiatry, International University of Health and Welfare, Tokyo, Japan.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Treatment‑resistant depression (TRD) reflects persistent dysfunction across large‑scale neural networks despite adequate pharmacotherapy. Neuromodulation offers mechanistically grounded interventions capable of directly modulating circuit‑level abnormalities implicated in TRD.

abstract.label: AREAS COVERED
abstract.text: This expert review synthesizes established, emerging, convulsive, and invasive neuromodulation modalities, including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), theta burst stimulation, accelerated TMS, deep TMS, transcranial electrical stimulation, temporal interference stimulation, photobiomodulation, low-field magnetic stimulation, transcranial focused ultrasound, electroconvulsive therapy, magnetic seizure therapy, vagus nerve stimulation, and deep brain stimulation. For each modality, technological foundations, mechanisms, efficacy, safety, and implementation considerations are summarized. Recent regulatory approvals of at-home prescription devices highlight the growing role of accessible home-based neuromodulation. Comparative effectiveness across effect size, tolerability, cost, and patient selection is reviewed. Advances in connectivity-informed targeting, tractography-guided neuromodulation, dose optimization, and biomarker-driven stratification illustrate the transition toward precision platforms. Literature for this review was identified through a non-systematic PubMed search.

abstract.label: EXPERT OPINION
abstract.text: Neuromodulation is evolving from a last-line intervention to a precision tool for circuit recalibration. Future progress will be driven by individualized targeting, closed-loop and multimodal stimulation, mechanistic trials, and scalable home-based delivery models. International collaborative research will be essential for validating biomarkers and accelerating development of next-generation circuit-based therapeutics.

title: Photobiomodulation and Migraine: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential.
first_affiliation: Hospital São Vicente de Paulo (HSVP), Bom Jesus do Itabapoana, Ribeirao Preto, Brazil.

abstract.text: Background: Migraine is a prevalent and disabling neurological disorder involving mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, altered cortical excitability, and neurovascular dysregulation. Photobiomodulation, a noninvasive intervention based on red or near-infrared light, has emerged as a promising strategy due to its multimodal biological effects.Objective: This narrative review aimed to synthesize current evidence on the biological mechanisms and therapeutic potential of photobiomodulation in migraine.Methods: A literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE for studies published up to June 2026, focusing on photobiomodulation, low-level laser therapy, migraine, headache, and related biological mechanisms.Results: Mechanistic evidence indicates that photobiomodulation enhances mitochondrial respiration, increases ATP production, restores redox homeostasis, and modulates nitric oxide signaling, contributing to improved cerebral perfusion and neurovascular coupling. In addition, photobiomodulation attenuates neuroinflammatory responses by reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines and glial activation while promoting neuroplasticity and cortical homeostasis. Preclinical models relevant to migraine, including trigeminovascular activation, nitroglycerin-induced hypersensitivity, and cortical spreading depression, support its translational plausibility by demonstrating reductions in hyperalgesia, oxidative stress, and neural inflammation.Conclusion: Although migraine-specific evidence remains limited, photobiomodulation represents a safe and potentially disease-modifying therapeutic approach. Future controlled clinical trials are needed to determine optimal stimulation parameters and clinical efficacy in migraine management.

title: Low-Level Laser Therapy Versus Mirror Therapy for Post-Stroke Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
journal: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy
first_affiliation: Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, NRS Medical College and Hospital, Kolkata, West Bengal, India.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome type 1 (CRPS-I) following stroke has been managed by several conservative methods to date. But the efficacy of Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) was never compared with the Mirror therapy (MT) in these cases.

abstract.label: AIM AND OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To compare the efficacy of LLLT versus MT in post-stroke CRPS-I.

abstract.label: MATERIAL AND METHODS
abstract.text: This comparative interventional study (Trial registration number: CTRI/2025/05/086943) was initially conducted with 47 patients with post-stroke CRPS-I after considering the inclusion and exclusion criteria. After obtaining informed consent, they were randomly divided into two groups. Along with kinesiotherapy in both the groups, LLLT was administered for Group 1 and MT for Group 2. Intensity of pain was measured by the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), and the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) was used for assessing sensorimotor recovery. All the variables were measured at the baseline, 4 weeks/visit 2, 8 weeks/visit 3 and 12 weeks/visit 4. A total of 44 cases (22 in each group) were analysed, as there were 3 dropouts on subsequent follow-ups.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Intra-group analysis showed significant improvement in both the parameters during all the follow-ups (p < 0.001). During inter group comparison, Group1 showed a significant improvement during follow-up at 4 weeks in terms of both pain intensity (Padj = 0.039) and sensorimotor recovery (Padj = 0.022), but subsequent follow-up visits showed no significant difference between the groups (Padj > 0.05).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: LLLT demonstrated an early between-group advantage over MT at 4 weeks in pain reduction and sensorimotor recovery in post-stroke CRPS-I. However, in the long run, no overall between-group superiority was noted, as both groups achieved comparable outcomes.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Institutional Scientific and Ethics committee (Reg. No: ECINEW/INST/2023/1862) approval no: NRSMC/IEC/149/2024.Trial Reg. no of this study under Clinical Trials Registry-India: CTRI/2025/05/086943.

title: The Glymphatic System in Neurological Diseases: Mechanisms, Imaging Surrogates, and Translational Uncertainties.
first_affiliation: School of Medicine, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA.

abstract.label: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
abstract.text: This narrative review critically synthesizes mechanistic, imaging, and clinical evidence on the glymphatic system in neurological disease. It distinguishes direct tracer-based observations from indirect imaging surrogates and identifies the principal uncertainties that currently limit clinical translation.

abstract.label: RECENT FINDINGS
abstract.text: The glymphatic framework describes glia-associated perivascular routes that support exchange between cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and interstitial fluid and contribute to solute transport in experimental models. Rodent studies show that aquaporin-4 polarization, vascular pulsatility, and sleep state modulate tracer movement, but the relative contribution of convection, diffusion, and alternative clearance pathways remains debated. Sleep-wake state alters interstitial or CSF concentrations of amyloid-beta and tau; however, these changes reflect both clearance and activity-dependent production or release. Meningeal lymphatic vessels interact anatomically and functionally with CSF drainage pathways in preclinical models, whereas direct evidence for an integrated glymphatic-meningeal circuit in humans remains limited. Most human disease studies use cross-sectional or longitudinal associations derived from indirect imaging markers rather than direct measurements of glymphatic flow. Intrathecal contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging provides a tracer-based assessment of CSF influx, distribution, and clearance to cervical lymph nodes. Diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space assesses water movement in the perivascular spaces, and phase-contrast MRI quantifies pulsatile CSF velocity and volume; both are noninvasive sequences. MRI-visible perivascular spaces, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, and CSF-hemodynamic coupling are indirect or partially overlapping measures of perivascular fluid biology. No noninvasive biomarker has yet been validated as a direct measure of human glymphatic flow. Candidate interventions including sleep-directed strategies, photobiomodulation, respiratory entrainment, gamma-frequency sensory stimulation, neuromodulation, and pharmacological approaches, remain preclinical or early mechanistic, and none has improved patient-important neurological outcomes through a validated glymphatic mechanism.

title: The importance of power in photobiomodulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of high-intensity laser therapy.
first_affiliation: Personalized Health Research Services, LLC, Winter Park, FL, United States.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Low-level laser therapy (LLLT; ≤ 0.5 W) is guideline-recommended in the United States for shallow-tissue oral mucositis and other superficial pathologies but has generally failed in trials for deeper tissue conditions due to limited penetration and subtherapeutic dosing. By contrast, Class IV high-intensity laser therapy (HILT; ≥ 0.5-80 W), typically at ∼100-fold higher power, has proven successful for many of these deeper tissue indications.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We systematically searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Database for Class IV HILT trials published from 2018 to April 2026, classifying interventions as effective when they showed large effect sizes (Cohen's d > 0.8).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Across 105 included studies (n = 2,710 HILT; n = 2,925 controls), no serious adverse events were reported. HILT reduced pain in all randomized trials of knee (k = 27), spine/neuromuscular (k = 20), shoulder/arm (k = 20), and wounds (k = 2), with > 90% showing large effect sizes. Additional benefits were observed in disorders of the feet (k = 13), hand/wrist (k = 8), face/jaw (k = 7), osteoporosis (k = 2), endometriosis, coronary artery disease, cognitive impairment, fibromyalgia, COVID-19, and obesity. HILT yielded durable analgesia, with large VAS pain reductions at end of treatment, < 3-month, and ≥ 3-month follow-ups (SMD -0.98, -1.18, and -1.01; k = 50, 19, and 21, respectively). Functional outcomes improved consistently, including range of motion (92%; k = 26), functional performance (84%; k = 57), and quality of life (85%; k = 25). Structural and physiological changes were observed, including increased knee cartilage thickness, reduced rotator cuff tear size, weight loss, and improved nerve conduction. Comparative trials showed HILT produced greater pain reduction than LLLT in 13/13 studies, all with large effect sizes. Mean HILT power was 9.3 W (median 10.0; range 0.5-30), and mean power density was 19.5 W/cm2 (median 10; range 0.1-52.5).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Class IV high-intensity laser therapy appears effective and safe for durable pain reduction across deep-tissue musculoskeletal pathologies, supporting its recognition in clinical practice and coverage by payers as a valuable therapeutic option. Further multicenter trials are needed to refine treatment protocols.

title: Photobiomodulation therapy and the regulation of excitation-inhibition balance in neurological and psychiatric disorders: Mechanistic and translational perspectives.
first_affiliation: Escola de Artes, Ciências e Humanidades da Universidade de São Paulo (USP), São Paulo, SP, Brazil; Instituto de Ciências Biomédicas, Universidade de São Paulo (USP), São Paulo, SP, Brazil.

abstract.text: Photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) has emerged as a promising non-invasive intervention capable of modulating biological processes through the application of non-ionizing light in the red to near-infrared spectrum. Increasing evidence suggests that PBMT may influence central nervous system (CNS) function through effects on mitochondrial activity, neurovascular coupling, and neuroimmune pathways. There is evidence that PBMT can attenuate cellular and molecular alterations and improve functional outcomes in different pathologies of the nervous system. Given that excitation-inhibition imbalance is a core pathophysiological mechanism underlying several neurological and psychiatric disorders, understanding the mechanistic and clinical effects of PBMT on neural network regulation is of growing scientific interest. This narrative review aims to synthesize mechanistic and translational evidence regarding the effects of PBMT on mechanisms relevant to excitation-inhibition regulation across neurological and psychiatric conditions. To our knowledge, this is the first review to specifically examine PBMT through the framework of excitation-inhibition balance across neurological and psychiatric disorders. Experimental studies have reported reductions in oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, attenuation of glutamatergic excitotoxicity and neuronal apoptosis, preservation of interneuron integrity, modulation of astrocytic function, and stimulation of neurogenesis. Early clinical findings suggest improvements in cognitive performance, mood symptoms, motor function, and behavioral outcomes. Overall, PBMT may influence mechanisms relevant to excitation-inhibition regulation through integrated mitochondrial, vascular, and immune mechanisms, supporting its potential as a systems-level neuromodulatory approach. Further research is required to consolidate translational evidence and clarify its potential role in clinical practice.

title: Comparative efficacy of neuromodulation techniques for Alzheimer's disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
first_affiliation: Department of Encephalopathy, The First Affiliated Hospital of Henan University of Chinese Medicine, Zhengzhou, China.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Neuromodulation techniques (NMTs) have shown potential therapeutic value in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the comparative efficacy of different modalities remains unclear. This study aimed to systematically compare and rank available NMTs to identify their relative benefits across cognitive, functional, and neuropsychiatric outcomes.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate and rank the efficacy of NMTs in improving cognitive function, activities of daily living (ADLs), and neuropsychiatric symptoms in AD patients, thereby providing evidence-based guidance for clinical intervention strategies.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: English-language literature was systematically searched in PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and EMBASE from database inception to February 2026. Inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of AD patients aged ≥18 years. Interventions included repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), photobiomodulation (PBM), transcutaneous electrical stimulation (TES), transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS), transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and sham stimulation (Sham). Outcome measures included Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Alzheimer' s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog), Alzheimer' s Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living (ADCS-ADL), Boston Naming Test (BNT), Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI), and Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS). Data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment followed Cochrane guidelines. Network meta-analysis (NMA) was conducted in Stata 17.0, with effect sizes ranked by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 36 RCTs involving 1,445 patients were included in the analysis. Compared with Sham, TPS significantly improved MMSE (MD = 3.92, 95% CI: 1.57 to 6.35; SUCRA = 97.50%), MoCA (MD = 4.99, 95% CI: 2.26 to 7.72; SUCRA = 69.25%), and BNT scores (MD = 4.02, 95% CI: 1.81 to 6.23; SUCRA = 81.8%). rTMS also showed favorable effects on ADAS-Cog scores (MD = -11.10, 95% CI: -14.51 to -7.71; SUCRA = 91.00%). Regarding activities of daily living, TES ranked highest on the ADCS-ADL scale (SUCRA = 71.00%). In terms of neuropsychiatric symptoms, TPS achieved the highest ranking for improving NPI scores (SUCRA = 92.3%), whereas tACS showed the best performance on GDS scores (SUCRA = 69.5%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Neuromodulation interventions demonstrated domain-specific benefits in AD, with no single approach showing universal superiority. TPS demonstrated the greatest potential for improving global cognitive outcomes, while rTMS showed advantages in ADAS-Cog performance. Nevertheless, limited sample sizes, heterogeneous stimulation protocols, and insufficient long-term evidence restrict the generalizability of current findings. Future multicenter RCTs with standardized protocols and prolonged follow-up are needed to confirm these results and guide clinical implementation.
